summary: Emil Kowalski argues that agents make engineers more leveraged than ever, but coding agents do not quite know what great visual work, such as animation, feels like, and that you can fix this by writing your taste down as strict rules in a skill file for each part of the interface. He shows that most taste decisions have a logical reason (for example, an element should grow from scale(0.95) rather than scale(0) because nothing in the real world appears from nothing). The article includes the exact rules from his own skills: a Practical Tips table for animation fixes, an easing decision flowchart, duration tiers with rules, and seven typography rules. For a design system this matters twice: the values themselves are concrete motion and typography defaults, and the method (articulate the why, set strict rules, hand them to agents) is how house standards get applied consistently by AI tools. [inferred]
key_ideas: Coding agents lack a sense of what great visual work feels like, so taste must be written down for them.
Write one skill file per aspect of the interface and give it to your agents.
Almost every taste decision has a logical reason; experience lets you name it, not just feel it.
Rules must be strict so the agent follows them instead of guessing or inventing its own.
Elements should enter from a slightly smaller scale (0.95), never from scale(0).
Easing is the most important part of an animation and is chosen with a fixed flowchart: enter or exit uses ease-out, on-screen movement uses ease-in-out, hover uses ease, constant motion uses linear.
UI animations stay under 300ms, scale with element size and travel distance, and exits can be about 20% faster than entrances.
Small CSS fixes solve common animation problems: scale(0.97) on press, will-change for jitter, animating a child to stop hover flicker, transform-origin at the trigger.
Typography taste can be packaged the same way: about 65ch body width, tabular numbers in price columns, loosened uppercase tracking, matched fallback fonts.
Underline only links, and use bold rather than italic for interface emphasis.
The creative part stays with the human; the more you package into a skill, the more leverage you get from agents.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: Encode taste as strict rules in one skill file per interface aspect so coding agents produce better visual work; use Anthropic's skill-creator; ask agents to review work against the skill.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Taste is explainable: with experience you can say why something feels better, and almost every taste decision has a logical reason.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Entering elements grow from scale(0.95), not scale(0), because real objects never appear from nothing (the balloon analogy).

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Easing is chosen by a strict flowchart (ease-out for enter/exit and default, ease-in-out for on-screen movement, ease for hover, linear for constant motion); durations are 100-150ms, 150-250ms or 200-300ms by element type, under 300ms overall, longer for larger elements and longer travel, exits about 20% faster.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Buttons get transform: scale(0.97) on :active; micro-interactions run 100-150ms; tooltips after the first one in a sequence skip their delay and animation.

topics.name: Animation performance
topics.summary: Add will-change: transform to fix shaky or jittery animations; a subtle blur under 20px can mask animations that still feel off.

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Popovers should scale from the trigger by setting transform-origin; modals and drawers animate in 200-300ms; he used his skill to have Claude Code improve a dialog animation.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Pressed buttons scale to 0.97 to feel responsive; small buttons get a 44px minimum hit area through a pseudo-element.

topics.name: Accessibility
topics.summary: Small buttons need a 44px minimum hit area; underlines are reserved for links so they stay a reliable affordance.

topics.name: Typography
topics.summary: Cap body text at about 65ch, use tabular-nums in price columns, use the ellipsis character, loosen uppercase letter-spacing, match fallback font metrics to avoid layout shift, reserve underline for links, prefer bold over italic for UI emphasis.

topics.name: Web implementation (CSS and React)
topics.summary: Rules are expressed as CSS: transform, :active, will-change, transform-origin, pseudo-element hit areas, blur, tabular-nums, ch units and the … character in markup.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Step back, ask why you made each decision, articulate it, set the rule and be strict, then feed the packaged rules to agents.

rules.rule: Make buttons feel responsive by adding transform: scale(0.97) on :active.
rules.why: Makes buttons feel responsive (the Practical Tips scenario it solves).
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Make buttons feel responsive

rules.rule: Animate entering elements from scale(0.95), never from scale(0).
rules.why: scale(0) looks like the element comes out of nowhere; a higher initial scale resembles the real world (a deflated balloon still has a visible shape) and feels more gentle, natural and elegant.
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Element appears from nowhere; Transferring taste

rules.rule: Fix shaky or jittery animations by adding will-change: transform.
rules.why: It is the listed fix for shaky or jittery animations; the source gives no further reason.

rules.rule: When a hover effect causes flicker, animate a child element instead of the hovered parent.
rules.why: It is the listed fix for hover-caused flicker; the source gives no further reason.

rules.rule: Set a popover's transform-origin to the location of its trigger so it scales out from the trigger.
rules.why: Otherwise the popover scales from the wrong point.
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Popover scales from wrong point

rules.rule: When tooltips open one after another, skip the delay and the animation for every tooltip after the first.
rules.why: Sequential tooltips feel slow when each one waits and animates.
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Sequential tooltips feel slow

rules.rule: Give small buttons a 44px minimum hit area, built with a pseudo-element.
rules.why: Small buttons are hard to tap.
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Small buttons hard to tap

rules.rule: If an animation still feels off after other fixes, add a subtle blur under 20px to mask it.
rules.why: Listed as the fix when something still feels off.
rules.evidence: Practical Tips: Something still feels off

rules.rule: Choose easing with the fixed decision flowchart every time, checking in order: entering or exiting the viewport, moving or morphing on screen, hover change, constant motion, then the default; do not improvise or invent easing rules.
rules.why: Easing is the most important part of any animation; the flowchart is strict so the agent doesn't have to guess or make up its own rules.

rules.rule: Use ease-out for any element entering or exiting the viewport.
rules.why: First branch of the easing flowchart.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart: entering or exiting the viewport

rules.rule: Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
rules.why: Easing flowchart branch for on-screen movement.
rules.evidence: Easing Decision Flowchart: moving/morphing on screen

rules.rule: Use ease for hover changes.
rules.why: Easing flowchart branch for hover changes.

rules.rule: Use linear for constant motion (the only flowchart branch that picks linear).
rules.why: Easing flowchart branch for constant motion.

rules.rule: When no flowchart branch applies, default to ease-out.
rules.why: The flowchart's default outcome.

rules.rule: Run micro-interactions for 100-150ms.
rules.why: Duration Guidelines table value for micro-interactions.

rules.rule: Run standard UI animations such as tooltips and dropdowns for 150-250ms.
rules.why: Duration Guidelines table value for standard UI.

rules.rule: Run modal and drawer animations for 200-300ms.
rules.why: Duration Guidelines table value for modals and drawers.

rules.rule: Keep every UI animation under 300ms.
rules.why: Stated as a duration rule.
rules.evidence: Duration Guidelines Rules: UI animations should stay under 300ms

rules.rule: Give larger elements longer durations than smaller ones.
rules.why: Stated as a duration rule: larger elements animate slower than smaller ones.
rules.evidence: Duration Guidelines Rules: Larger elements animate slower

rules.rule: Make exit animations about 20% faster than the matching entrance.
rules.why: Stated as a duration rule: exits can be ~20% faster than entrance.
rules.evidence: Duration Guidelines Rules: Exit animations can be ~20% faster

rules.rule: Match duration to distance: the longer the element travels, the longer the duration.
rules.why: Stated as a duration rule.
rules.evidence: Duration Guidelines Rules: Match duration to distance

rules.rule: Cap body text at about 65ch instead of letting it stretch full width.
rules.why: Keeps line length comfortable to read.

rules.rule: Apply tabular-nums to price columns.
rules.why: Digits align and the column reads cleanly.

rules.rule: Use the … character in markup instead of three periods (...).

rules.rule: Loosen letter-spacing on uppercase labels.

rules.rule: Declare a fallback font stack whose x-height and weight match the primary face.

decisions.question: Which easing curve should an animation use?

options.name: ease-out
options.effect: Starts fast and settles [inferred]; the flowchart's choice for entering and exiting.
options.when: The element is entering or exiting the viewport, or no other branch applies (default).

options.name: ease-in-out
options.when: The element is moving or morphing on screen.

decisions.recommendation: Pick by the job of the animation using the strict flowchart, defaulting to ease-out; easing is the most important part of any animation. Grouping curves by job matches the role-based option [inferred].

decisions.question: What scale should an element start from when it appears?

options.name: scale(0)
options.effect: Looks like the element comes out of nowhere; feels wrong.

options.name: scale(0.95)
options.effect: Gentle, natural and elegant, like a deflated balloon that still has a shape.
options.when: Any element that appears or enters.

decisions.recommendation: Start from scale(0.95), not scale(0), because a higher initial value resembles the real world.
decisions.evidence: Transferring taste; Practical Tips: Element appears from nowhere

decisions.question: How long should a UI animation run?

options.name: 150-250ms
options.effect: The middle tier; a short, noticeable transition [inferred].
options.when: Standard UI such as tooltips and dropdowns.

options.name: 200-300ms
options.effect: The longest tier; larger elements animate slower than smaller ones.

decisions.recommendation: Use the tier for the element type, stay under 300ms, go longer for larger elements and longer travel, and make exits about 20% faster than entrances.

decisions.question: How wide can body text run?

options.name: Full width
options.effect: Lines stretch across the container and become uncomfortable to read.

decisions.recommendation: Cap body text at about 65ch so line length stays comfortable to read.

decisions.question: Should digits in price columns all be the same width?

options.name: Default digits
options.effect: Digits may not line up down the column [inferred].

options.name: tabular-nums
options.effect: Digits align and the column reads cleanly.

decisions.question: How should important non-link text stand out?

options.name: Underline
options.effect: Looks clickable; weakens underline as the link affordance and tempts clicks on inert copy.

options.name: Italic
options.effect: Reads like print editorial, not UI hierarchy.
options.when: Citations and linguistic stress in prose.

decisions.recommendation: Use weight or color (bold) for emphasis, underline only for links, italic only for citations and stress in prose.

decisions.question: How big should the tappable area of a small button be?

options.name: Same as the visible button
options.effect: Small buttons are hard to tap.

options.name: 44px minimum hit area
options.effect: Easier to tap; built with a pseudo-element so the visible size can stay small [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Use a 44px minimum hit area via a pseudo-element.
decisions.evidence: Practical Tips: Small buttons hard to tap

process.detail: With experience, work out not only which version feels better but why, until you can articulate it.
Step back from each decision and ask why you made it; almost every taste decision has a logical reason.
Create a skill file for each aspect of the interface (animation, layout, icons, color theory, typography) that describes the rules.

State each rule so the agent does not have to guess, as in his examples: a scenario and solution table (Practical Tips), a decision flowchart (easing), a duration table with rules, and numbered typography rules each with its reason.
Use Anthropic's skill-creator skill to make packaging the rules easier.
Give the skill to your coding agents and ask them to improve work, e.g. a dialog animation; the agent returns a list of issues based on your rules and a before and after table of what changed.
The more creative part of the job stays with you; package everything else to get more leverage from agents.

caveats: Opens with a plug for his course aiforui.dev (early access closed) and ends with a 'Get the skill' plug for one big design engineering skill made from his blog articles (animations, component design, principles from open-source projects like Sonner); neither is a rule.
Publication date is unknown, so tool references (Claude Code, Anthropic's skill-creator) may be dated.
Several demos (the Linear logo, the Options scale comparison, the Claude Code dialog video) are embedded media; the text only describes them, so their exact motion values are not captured.
Some rules are worded permissively in the source: exits 'can be' ~20% faster, and the blur under 20px is a masking fix for when 'something still feels off', not a default.
The easing flowchart is presented as 'my philosophy'; it names only CSS keyword curves (ease-out, ease-in-out, ease, linear) and gives no cubic-bezier values.
The stated reason for the … character (truncation following the container instead of a fixed character count) is copied as given and not explained further in the text.
Small tension in the source: the rule says UI animations should stay under 300ms, while the modal and drawer tier is 200-300ms, whose top end equals 300ms.
The article shows excerpts of his skill files ('some rules on typography', 'many others live under Practical Tips'), not the complete skills.

Strengths follow the source's framing: Practical Tips rows are problem and fix tips (should), except where the alternative is called wrong (scale(0), popover scaling from the wrong point); the easing flowchart is called strict and the duration 'Rules' and typography 'rules' are labelled rules (must), except permissive wording ('can be', 'Prefer').
